clinicalPearls: A congenital, usually unilateral optic disc dysplasia resembling the morning glory flower, with a funnel-shaped excavated disc
The enlarged disc has a central glial tuft, an elevated surrounding annulus of chorioretinal pigment, and radially arranged vessels emerging like spokes
Often detected on investigation of poor vision, strabismus or leukocoria in early childhood
Associated with midline cranial and central nervous system anomalies, including basal encephalocoele, absent corpus callosum and pituitary abnormalities
Part of the PHACE association and linked to moyamoya-type cerebral vasculopathy, warranting cerebral vascular imaging
Serous retinal detachment is a recognised complication that can further reduce vision
Midfacial anomalies (hypertelorism, cleft lip/palate) should prompt a search for a basal encephalocoele
reference.pathophysiology: Morning glory disc anomaly is thought to arise from defective closure of the posterior scleral wall and abnormal development of the optic nerve head and surrounding neuroectodermal and mesodermal tissues. The result is a large, funnel-shaped excavation of the disc with a central glial remnant, a raised pigmented peripapillary ring and anomalous radiating retinal vessels. Because these structures develop alongside midline forebrain and vascular elements, the anomaly is frequently accompanied by midline brain defects, hypothalamic-pituitary dysfunction and cerebral arterial anomalies such as moyamoya. Traction and abnormal tissue at the disc predispose to serous (often non-rhegmatogenous) retinal detachment.
additionalInvestigations: MRI of the brain and orbits to detect midline anomalies and encephalocoele
MR or CT angiography for moyamoya-type cerebral vasculopathy
OCT and fundus imaging of the disc and macula
Assessment for serous retinal detachment with dilated examination
Paediatric and, where indicated, neurosurgical review
redFlags: Midfacial dysmorphism suggesting a transsphenoidal basal encephalocoele
Neurological symptoms or signs of cerebral ischaemia from moyamoya vasculopathy
Features of hypopituitarism such as hypoglycaemia or growth failure
New serous retinal detachment causing acute visual decline
Nasal mass or CSF rhinorrhoea indicating an encephalocoele
reference.prognosis: Vision in the affected eye is usually poor and often does not improve, and serous detachment can worsen it; systemic outcome depends on the associated central nervous system, vascular and endocrine anomalies.
pitfalls: Treating the disc anomaly as an isolated ocular finding and omitting neuroimaging
Missing moyamoya vasculopathy that carries a stroke risk
Overlooking pituitary dysfunction and endocrine deficits
Mistaking a serous detachment for a rhegmatogenous one and mismanaging it
references: Taylor & Hoyt's Paediatric Ophthalmology and Strabismus
management: Cerebral vascular imaging with MR or CT angiography and ongoing surveillance for moyamoya-type vasculopathy, with neurosurgical revascularisation if it progresses
Neuroimaging for midline and central nervous system anomalies such as basal encephalocoele and agenesis of the corpus callosum, with neurosurgical management of an encephalocoele
Endocrine assessment of pituitary function with hormone replacement for hypothalamic-pituitary dysfunction
Amblyopia management with refractive correction and occlusion, and treatment of associated strabismus
Monitor for and treat serous retinal detachment, which may require laser or surgical intervention
Low-vision support given the typically poor and non-improving vision in the affected eye
Multidisciplinary paediatric ophthalmology, neurology and neurosurgery and endocrinology, with genetic assessment for associated conditions
